headline: Scientists Discover Plastic-Eating Enzyme That Works Like Pac-Man
meta_description: Researchers at University of Konstanz discovered an enzyme that helps bacteria break down biodegradable plastics in soil within a year, offering new hope again…
summary_short: A newly discovered enzyme nicknamed 'Pac-Man' helps bacteria devour certain plastics. Biodegradable materials completely broke down in soil within 9-11 months.
body:
Researchers at the University of Konstanz have discovered a remarkable enzyme that could transform how we tackle plastic waste. The enzyme, nicknamed the "Pac-Man enzyme" for its distinctive wide molecular opening, enables bacteria to break down certain biodegradable plastics far more efficiently than previously known. In experiments conducted in forest soil at the university's botanical garden, bioplastics buried roughly ten centimeters deep completely degraded within nine to eleven months—a striking contrast to conventional high-density polyethylene, which showed virtually no decomposition over the same period.

Biologists Harry Lerner and David Schleheck studied long-chain aliphatic polyesters, a biodegradable material developed by chemist Stefan Mecking. By analyzing microbial communities in soil and tracking carbon dioxide release as microorganisms consumed the plastics, they discovered that while cellulose broke down in about eighty days, the bioplastics required 250 to 330 days for complete degradation. The findings suggest bacteria are adapting to digest certain plastics more rapidly than scientists believed possible.

Yet the discovery reveals both promise and limitation. The enzyme unexpectedly showed the ability to break down penicillin, hinting at possible connections to antibiotic resistance—a reminder that biological solutions require careful study. More significantly, for bacteria to make a meaningful dent in global plastic pollution, we would need far more products manufactured from biodegradable materials with chemical bonds microbes can actually break apart. The research, published in The ISME Journal, offers hope that nature's own mechanisms might help us solve a problem we created—but only if we fundamentally change what plastics we produce.
